paper_title: JoVox: Joint Hierarchical Flow Matching for Lightweight Voxel Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or lightweight but of lower fidelity. Hierarchical methods keep the lightweight nature of voxels. However, their coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited, so they are often plausible but wrong. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level, so that coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated nearby. Within this framework, we further introduce a two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer at once instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity. We also introduce an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models. Our framework outperforms the baselines on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8x higher training throughput, 1/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 4 vs. 32 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11% lower Chamfer distance.

Introduction Voxel generation is an important problem in computer vision. Voxels record where 3D shape lies in space, giving lightweight and widely used 3D representation. For example, existing models can turn voxels into fine-grained 3D shapes [30, 31], keeping the structure that the voxels define. Yet generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping this lightweight nature remains an open problem. Existing methods address this problem in two ways. Latent methods [30, 31] achieve high fidelity by compressing the voxel grid with an autoencoder and generating the latent grid with generator. The autoencoder is an extra model to train, and the generator still processes every cell of the latent grid, including those in empty space, so the computational cost remains high. Hierarchical methods [9, 27, 33] instead generate coarse grid first and refine its occupied cells into finer grids, level by level, which keeps the lightweight nature of voxels. However, the coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited. They are thus often plausible but wrong, and the finer levels inherit these errors. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in decid1 ing coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the hierarchy, instead of separate distribution for each level as in hierarchical methods [9, 27, 33]. Such distribution is hard to model, since the structure of the hierarchy varies across shapes, with finer cells only inside occupied cells. We model it with masked discrete flow matching [7, 11], which unmasks few cells at each step, at any level of the hierarchy, and grows the hierarchy as cells are unmasked. coarse cell that is still masked can then be predicted with the finer cells already unmasked nearby. Our framework needs no autoencoder and processes only the cells inside occupied cells, which keeps generation lightweight. Within this framework, we further introduce two-level prediction and an unmasking strategy. Two-level prediction outputs the cells two levels finer at once, instead of one level finer as in hierarchical methods [6, 9, 27], and thus halves the number of levels that the network processes. We also find that two-level prediction yields voxels of higher fidelity (Section 5.4). Our unmasking strategy remasks the oldest unmasked cells, which were decided with the fewest finer cells around them, so that they are revisited once finer cells are generated. This also corrects the inconsistencies of cells unmasked in the same step [3, 12]. We evaluate our method on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation, where it outperforms current SOTA. In particular, our framework makes training far cheaper than that of TRELLIS.2 [31]. With the same backbone, our framework needs significantly less GPU memory and has 8 higher training throughput (Figure 5), while its voxels remain of higher fidelity, with an 11% lower Chamfer distance. In summary, our contributions are as follows. JoVox, discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint hierarchical distribution of voxels while keeping generation lightweight. Two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity, and an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models [3, 12]. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8 higher training throughput, 1/15 of the FLOPs in forward pass, train on 4 vs. 32 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11% lower Chamfer distance. 2. Related work Voxel generation. Voxels are generated as the first stage of many 3D generators [2932], or obtained by voxelizing the meshes of 3D generators that produce meshes directly [10, 24]. Methods that generate voxels fall into two Table 1. Comparison of voxel generation methods. Method TRELLIS, TRELLIS.2 LAS-Diffusion DVD XCube Nexus, OctFusion Octree Transformer, OAT OctGPT Ours Hierarchy No autoencoder Parallel Joint levels groups, dense methods and hierarchical methods. Dense methods generate every cell of full grid. TRELLIS [30, 31] compresses the voxels into compact latent grid with an autoencoder and generates this latent grid, which reaches high fidelity at the cost of training an additional autoencoder. LAS-Diffusion [37] and DVD [32] instead generate the occupancy grid directly. LAS-Diffusion generates the occupancy with continuous diffusion and thresholds the result. DVD treats the occupancy as discrete data and generates it with discrete diffusion. Since all these methods generate every cell, including those in empty space, their cost grows with the cube of the resolution. Hierarchical methods generate the voxels level by level and refine only occupied cells, which skips empty space. XCube [19] generates sparse voxel hierarchy, with its own latent diffusion model and autoencoder at each level. Nexus [26] and OctFusion [33] generate the octree with continuous diffusion and threshold the result to decide which cells to refine. Octree Transformer [9] and OAT [6] generate the octree autoregressively, one cell at time, so the number of forward passes grows with the number of cells. OctGPT [27] generates many cells of level in parallel by masking. However, it decides the finer cells inside cell independently and needs many steps at every level. In all these methods, coarse level is decided from the coarser levels alone. Such level is only roughly plausible. We instead learn the joint distribution of all levels, so that finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. Each prediction also outputs the cells two levels finer, instead of one level finer. Like the hierarchical methods above, we refine only occupied cells. We generate the occupancy itself, without an autoencoder. Table 1 summarizes these differences. Discrete diffusion and flow matching. Masked discrete diffusion models [2, 5, 14, 21] and discrete flow matching [7, 11] generate discrete data by unmasking masked sequence over several steps, and have been applied to text and image tokens. These data have fixed size, whereas voxel hierarchy grows as its cells are unmasked. We extend masked discrete flow matching to such hierarchy. When several tokens are unmasked in one step, these models sample them independently, which can make them inconsistent with each other. Some works model the dependence among the tokens unmasked together [8, 12, 34]. 2 Other works choose which tokens to unmask together [3, 15, 20, 28], or remask unmasked tokens so that they can be revised [25]. Our unmasking strategy also remasks, but chooses the oldest unmasked cells, which were decided with the fewest finer cells around them. 3. Two-level prediction Hierarchical methods such as Octree Transformer [9] define the occupancy code of cell as the occupancy of its eight children, which has 8 bits. They process cell to predict its occupancy code, one level finer, instead of its own occupancy as in Section 4.1. We call this single-level prediction. In our framework, single-level prediction uses the formulation of Section 4.1 with occupancy codes in place of occupancies. The entries xi = {0, 1}8 are the occupancy codes at the levels = {0, . . . , 1}. The data sample x1 contains the occupancy codes of the cells at level 0 and of the occupied cells at the levels 1, . . . , 1. We mask the occupancy codes as in Section 4.1 to obtain xt, where Cl(xt) is now the set of occupancy codes at level in xt. Once cell at the levels 1, . . . , 1 is known to be occupied, we add its masked occupancy code to xt. In two-level prediction, the model instead processes cell at level 2 to predict the occupancy of its 4 4 4 cells two levels finer, at level + 2 (Figure 2 (a)). One possible way is to use the occupancy of these cells as one entry, but such an entry would take 264 values, which is prohibitively large. We therefore split the occupancy of these cells into eight 8-bit occupancy codes, one for each child of u, each giving the occupancy of the eight cells at level + 2 inside that child. For cell u, the model thus takes these eight occupancy codes, masked or unmasked, as input and outputs eight distributions of Equation (6), each over the 28 values of an occupancy code, instead of one distribution over 264 values. Specifically, we take to be even and let the cells lie at the even levels 0, 2, . . . , 2, so that the entries are the occupancy codes at the odd levels = {1, 3, . . . , 1}. The data sample x1 contains the 8-bit occupancy codes of the eight children of every cell at level 0 and of every occupied cell at the levels 2, . . . , 2. We mask the occupancy codes as in single-level prediction to obtain xt. Once cell at the levels 2, . . . , 2 is known to be occupied, we add the masked occupancy codes of its eight children to xt. The model thus processes each cell at level 0 and each cell known to be occupied. Two-level prediction thus processes cells at only half of the levels of single-level prediction, so training is faster (Section 5.4). 4.3. We draw the tl of different levels independently, so the network is trained on any combination of fractions across levels. The intermediate states xt produced by any unmasking strategy therefore lie within the training distribution. Finer levels have far more occupancy codes than coarser ones, so loss summed over all occupancy codes would be dominated by the finer levels. We therefore first average the loss over the occupancy codes of each level, and then average over the levels. Unmasking strategy Occupancy codes unmasked in the same step are sampled independently, each from its predicted probabilities, so they may be inconsistent with each other [3, 8, 12, 34]. Some samplers for masked generation correct such inconsistencies by remasking unmasked entries, so that these entries 5 are predicted again [25]. Our strategy also remasks, and chooses the occupancy codes to remask by when they were unmasked. Occupancy codes unmasked early are sampled given few unmasked occupancy codes. This holds in particular for coarse occupancy codes, which are unmasked before most finer occupancy codes exist. Our strategy therefore remasks the oldest unmasked occupancy codes at each step, so that they are predicted again given the occupancy codes unmasked after them, including finer occupancy codes in nearby cells. Generation starts from x0 and runs for steps = 0, . . . , 1. At step k, the target fraction of unmasked occupancy codes at level is given by the schedule κl(k) = min(k/Nl, 1)ρ, (9) which reaches 1 at = Nl . Finer occupancy codes are added as coarser ones are unmasked, so we let the schedules of coarser levels reach 1 earlier, N1 N3 NL1 = . Early in generation, with few occupancy codes unmasked, the predictions are least certain, so occupancy codes unmasked in the same step are most likely to be inconsistent with each other. We therefore use ρ > 1, so that κl grows slowly at first and quickly later. Each step does three things in order. First, for 1, each level remasks its oldest unmasked occupancy codes, so that its fraction of unmasked occupancy codes goes back to about κl(k 1). When an occupancy code is remasked, the cells that it marked as occupied are no longer known to be occupied. As in Section 4.1, the occupancy codes of all cells inside them are then removed from xt. Second, the network predicts all masked occupancy codes in xt, with each tl set to the fraction of unmasked occupancy codes at level l. Third, each level unmasks masked occupancy codes chosen at random, so that its fraction rises to about κl(k + 1). To unmask an occupancy code, we sample its value from the probabilities predicted in the second step, at temperature τ . At τ = 0, we take the most probable value. Under the schedule, very large number of occupancy codes at level 1 would be unmasked in step 1, and these would likely be inconsistent with each other. To alleviate this, we add few extra steps after step 1 and unmask these occupancy codes evenly over step 1 and the extra steps. The extra steps do not remask. See Section in the appendix for details. 5. Experiments We evaluate our framework on image-conditioned generation (Section 5.1) and unconditional generation (Section 5.2), measure its efficiency (Section 5.3), and ablate its designs (Section 5.4). All shapes are represented by their 643 surface occupancy, the finest level of hierarchy with = 4. We also show shapes generated at higher resolution of 2563 by our framework with = 6 in Section of the appendix. We run all baselines in Sections 5.1 and 5.2 with their official weights and settings, and evaluate all methods on the same test data with the same metrics in each task. Details of the data and metrics are provided in the appendix. 5.1. Image-conditioned generation Data. We train on 174,528 assets of TRELLIS-500K [30] and test on 1,000 objects of Toys4k [23], which are unseen during training. The condition is rendered view of each asset. Baselines. We compare with TRELLIS.2 [31], the state of the art, and with TRELLIS [30], DVD [32], Direct3DS2 [29], TripoSG [10] and TripoSR [24]. Voxels are often used to generate meshes, so we evaluate both the voxels and the meshes of each method. TRELLIS, DVD, TRELLIS.2, our framework and Direct3D-S2 generate 643 voxels. For the first four, we obtain the meshes by passing the voxels through the mesh stage of TRELLIS.2, which generates mesh from 643 voxels. Direct3D-S2 refines its voxels into mesh with its own second stage, and we evaluate this mesh. TripoSG and TripoSR generate meshes directly, and their voxel metrics use these meshes voxelized at 643. Metrics. We first align each generated shape to its ground truth in orientation and scale, and then compare it with the ground truth. On the voxels, we report the voxel Chamfer distance (CDV) and the voxel IoU, which measure geometric accuracy. few misplaced voxels barely change these two metrics but produce visible artifacts, so we also report the LPIPS (LPIPSV) and DINOv2 [17] similarity (DINOV) between renderings of the generated and groundtruth voxels, which measure perceptual similarity. On the meshes, we report (i) CDshell, the Chamfer distance between the outer surfaces, which measures geometric accuracy, (ii) LPIPSN and CLIPN [18] on rendered normal maps, which measure perceptual similarity, and (iii) the Uni3D [38] similarity of point clouds sampled on the meshes, which measures semantic similarity. Results. As shown in Table 2, our framework achieves the best value on every voxel metric. Compared with TRELLIS.2, its voxels have an 11% lower Chamfer distance and an IoU of 0.416 against 0.402, and their renderings have the highest perceptual similarity to the ground truth. Since TRELLIS, DVD, TRELLIS.2 and our framework share one mesh stage, their meshes differ only in the voxels they start from. Our voxels thus lead to 22% lower CDshell than those of TRELLIS.2 and to the lowest LPIPSN (Figure 3). 5.2. Unconditional generation Data. We use the chair, airplane, table and rifle categories of ShapeNet [4], with the training and test splits of LASDiffusion [37]. The test split of each category, voxelized at 643, serves as its reference set. Baselines. We compare with LAS-Diffusion, OctFusion [33], OctGPT [27] and XCube [19]. XCube releases models only for chair and airplane, so we compare with it on these two categories. LAS-Diffusion generates 643 occupancy, and XCube generates sparse 5123 occupancy, which we max-pool to 643. OctFusion and OctGPT output 323 occupancy and mesh. We evaluate both outputs of these two methods, voxelizing the meshes at 643 in the same way as the reference sets. Rows that use the 323 occupancy are marked in the tables. Metrics. Unconditional samples have no corresponding ground truth, so we compare the generated set of each category with its reference set. We report the 1-NNA, the coverage (COV) and the minimum matching distance (MMD) [1, 35], which measure distribution similarity, diversity and fidelity, respectively, all computed with the Chamfer distance between voxel centers. We also report FIDV on PointNet++ features of Point-E [16], and FIDVD and KIDVD on DINOv2 features of voxel renderings, which measure the distance between the generated and reference distributions in 3D feature space and an image feature space, respectively. Results. As shown in Table 3, our framework achieves the best value on all six metrics, averaged over the four categories. Its FIDV is 80% lower and its FIDVD is 64% lower than the best baseline values. OctFusion, OctGPT and XCube are hierarchical methods, whose coarse levels are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited. Our framework learns the joint distribution of all levels and outperforms OctFusion and OctGPT on the four categories and XCube on chair and airplane. Table 7 in the appendix gives the results of each category. Figure 4 shows chairs generated by our framework, with fine and complex structures. 5.3. Efficiency We compare one training step (a forward pass, backward pass and an optimizer update) of our network and of the voxel stage of TRELLIS.2 with the same backbone. Both run on one A100 GPU with 80 GB, with gradient checkpointing, fp32 master weights and bf16 mixed precision. As shown in Figure 5, at batch size of 32 our framework needs 29.0 GB of GPU memory instead of 47.3 GB and has 8 higher training throughput, and it can be trained with batch sizes at which TRELLIS.2 runs out of memory. Since the two networks share the backbone, these differences in memory and throughput come from the number of cells they process. After about two days of training (80K steps), our framework surpasses TRELLIS, which is trained for 400K steps, on every metric of Section 5.1. After about two and half days, it matches TRELLIS.2 (Table 9 in the appendix), whose paper does not report the number of training steps. Our framework also generates the voxels faster than the voxel stage of TRELLIS.2 (Table 6 in the appendix). 5.4. Ablation studies To measure the cost of full training, we train our framework on four H100 GPUs with batch size of 256. TRELWe conduct ablation studies on image-conditioned generation on Toys4k. 7 Figure 4. Unconditional generation of chairs by our framework on ShapeNet. Unmasking strategy. We compare our unmasking strategy with other samplers, all applied to our model of Section 5.1. MDLM [21] does not remask. ReMDM [25] remasks unmasked occupancy codes chosen at random, and its confidence-based variant ReMDM-conf [25] remasks the less confident ones with higher probability. MaskGIT [5] unmasks the most probable occupancy codes first and does not remask. Unlike these samplers, our strategy chooses the occupancy codes to remask by when they were unmasked. An occupancy code unmasked earlier is predicted given fewer finer occupancy codes in nearby cells, so its prediction is less certain. Our strategy therefore remasks the oldest unmasked occupancy codes, so that they are revisited once finer occupancy codes are unmasked. As shown in Table 5, our strategy gives the lowest voxel Chamfer distance and the highest IoU among all samplers. 6. Limitations and future work limitation of our model is the size of its training set. Due to limited training resources, we train it on about 175K assets, less than quarter of the roughly 800K assets used to train TRELLIS.2 [31]. While our model, with the data augmentation described in the appendix, still outperforms TRELLIS.2 in generalization to the unseen objects of Toys4k, we expect more training data to further improve it. Besides, like other masked discrete flow matching models, our model unmasks multiple occupancy codes independently in one step, which can make them inconsistent with each other [3, 8, 12, 34]. Our unmasking strategy is designed to reduce such inconsistencies, and exploring better unmasking strategies may further improve the quality of the generated voxels. In future work, we plan to apply our framework to generating large scenes with multiple objects and long sequences of 3D shapes. Both contain far more voxels than single object, and our framework keeps their training lightweight by processing only the cells inside occupied cells. 7. Conclusion We presented JoVox, discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, so that finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. Within this framework, two-level prediction halves the number of levels that the network processes and yields voxels of higher fidelity, and our unmasking strategy Figure 5. Peak GPU memory and training throughput of our network and of the voxel stage of TRELLIS.2, with the same backbone, at each batch size on one A100 GPU with 80 GB. cross marks the batch size at which TRELLIS.2 runs out of memory. Table 5. Ablation of the unmasking strategy on Toys4k. The best and second-best values of each column are in bold and underlined, respectively. Sampler MDLM [21] ReMDM [25] ReMDM-conf [25] MaskGIT [5] Ours CDV 0.01162 0.01115 0.01116 0.01243 0.01107 IoU 0.4035 0.4085 0.4139 0.3987 0.4158 Two-level prediction and joint hierarchical modeling. We compare our framework with two variants in Table 4. The single-level variant uses single-level prediction (Section 4.2) and the two-level variant uses two-level prediction, and both generate the hierarchy level by level. By contrast, ours extends the two-level variant with joint hierarchical modeling. All three share the network architecture and the training data, and are trained for the same number of steps, fewer than those used for our model in Section 5.1. As shown in Table 4, the two-level variant improves every metric over the single-level variant. Compared with the two-level variant, our framework lowers the voxel Chamfer distance by 22% and CDshell by 32%, and improves every metric. In addition, two-level prediction makes training faster, since the network processes fewer tokens. With both variants on four A100 GPUs at batch size of 256, one training step of the two-level variant takes 4.03 s, compared with 8.96 for the single-level variant, 2.2 speedup. 8 revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated. Our framework outperforms the baselines on unconditional and image-conditioned generation, while its training is far cheaper than that of TRELLIS.2. Our results thus show that voxels can be generated with both clearly improved fidelity and drastically improved efficiency.

Generation at 2563 Figure 6 shows shapes generated at 2563 from input images by our framework with = 6 (Section B). B. Implementation details The experiments in Section 5 use = 4, so the finest level is grid of 643 cells. The tokens come from the cells at level 0 and the occupied cells at level 2, with grids of 43 and 163 cells, and the occupancy codes are at levels 1 and 3. The 2563 shapes in Section and on the project webpage are generated by model with = 6, where the tokens come from the cells at level 0 and the occupied cells at levels 2 and 4, and the occupancy codes are at levels 1, 3 and 5. For this model, we add the level embedding emblevel(4) and the embedding emb 5 of t5, initialize all other weights from the model with = 4, and train it for 32K further steps on four GPUs. The transformer has 1.54B parameters in 30 blocks of width 1536 with 12 heads. The image encoder is frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 at resolution of 512 512. The condition is dropped with probability 0.1 during training, and classifier-free guidance at scale 1.5 is applied to the logits during sampling. We train with AdamW [13] at learning rate of 104 and batch size of 256 on four GPUs, and keep an exponential moving average of the weights. For data augmentation, the condition image is randomly perturbed in brightness, saturation, contrast, hue and gamma, and the occupancy is rotated by random multiple of 90 about the vertical axis. We draw tl = l with vl U(0, 1). In the unmasking strategy of Section 4.5, we remask at the levels one after another at each step, from the coarsest to the finest, so that we count the unmasked occupancy codes at finer level only after remasking at the coarser levels has removed some of them. At step 1, at each level with κl(k) < 1, we remask up to round (cid:0)(1κl(k 1)/κl(k)) n(cid:1) occupancy codes, rounded half to even, where is the number of all unmasked occupancy codes at level l. We do not remask an occupancy code unmasked at step 1, since no prediction has yet been made given it, nor an occupancy code unmasked in step in which no other occupancy code, at any level, was unmasked. Among the other unmasked occupancy codes, we remask those last unmasked earliest, with ties broken at random, or all of them if there are fewer. For the prediction, we set tl to 0 at level that has no occupancy codes. After the prediction, we unmask only occupancy codes predicted at this step, and occupancy codes added after an unmasking are first predicted at the next step and are not counted below.
